title: Probe sweeps for model onboarding: latency / cost / quality sensitivity
content:
Summary:
This note captures a targeted set of probe sweeps we ran as part of a model onboarding triage for two open-source decoder models (model-A-lite and model-B-13B). The goal: map the 3-way tradeoff surface (latency, per-token cost, and end-to-end quality) across batching, prefix/KV caching priming, and max_tokens caps — while keeping the evaluation promptset and regression detection hooks identical to the onboarding harness used by Product Evals.

Key motivation and constraints:
- Onboarding stage: we want a compact signal that flags models which will likely violate product SLOs or cause large cost regressions when used at scale.
- SLOs: p95 generation latency < 250ms (interactive chat), median per-token inference cost < baseline * 1.8 for hosted tier.
- Quality regression detection: use the canonical promptset (n=240 prompts, mixture of short chat, long-form summarization, and code-completion). We compute task-specific metrics (BLEU/ROUGE for summarization, pass@k for code snippets, and human-like semantic score proxy using eval-model-v2).
- Hardware: tests run on ded-rtx8000 (single-GPU) to simplify kernel selection effects.

Experiment grid (probe design):
- Batching: {1, 2, 4, 8} requests per micro-batch (continuous batching enabled in runtime).
- KV/Prefix caching modes: {none, warm-prefix-cache, kv-prefetch} where warm-prefix-cache means we pre-seed KV cache with the prompt prefixes for the top 50% of repeating prompts; kv-prefetch triggers a background precompute for expected next-token prefixes (experimental).
- max_tokens generation cap: {64, 128, 256, 512}.
- Temperature fixed at 0.7, sampling top_k=50 for open models.
- Each sweep cell: 240 prompts × 5 seeds for stochastic sampling (where applicable). We collect latency (p50/p95/p99), tokens generated, GPU time, and model quality metrics per prompt.

Notable design choices (non-standard):
- Prompt heterogeneity bucketization: we binary-bucket prompts into low-context (<=64 input tokens) and high-context (>64 input tokens) to reveal caching impact. Many prior runs average across prompt length which masks cache benefits.
- Regression sensitivity metric: define a composite "regression score" = max(0, relative_cost_increase * 0.6 + relative_quality_drop * 0.4). We mark any cell with regression score > 0.15 as a red flag for downstream product reviews.

High-level results (selected highlights):
- Baseline (model-A-lite, batch=1, no-cache, max_tokens=256): p95 latency = 210ms, median per-token cost = baseline_unit*1.0, quality proxy = 0.78 (on 0-1).
- Batch effects: batching up to 4 reduces median per-token cost by ~22% relative to batch=1 but increases p95 latency nonlinearly for high-context prompts: p95 moves from 210ms→340ms at batch=4 for high-context prompts. For low-context prompts p95 stays below 260ms even at batch=4.
- Caching effects: warm-prefix-cache reduces p95 for high-context prompts by ~26% (e.g., 340ms→250ms at batch=4), and reduces GPU time per prompt by ~18%. kv-prefetch gives additional ~6% cost reduction but increased variance (occasional p99 spikes) — flagged as unstable.
- max_tokens cap: moving from 512→128 reduces average tokens generated by 42% (expected) and yields cost drop ~40% with small quality loss on short-completion prompts (quality proxy drop 0.02). For long-form summarization, clipping at 128 caused quality to drop 0.12, which triggered regression flags even when cost improved.

Example numeric slice (model-A-lite, high-context prompts):
- batch=1, no-cache, max_tokens=256: p50=95ms, p95=210ms, p99=480ms, cost/unit=1.0, quality=0.78
- batch=4, no-cache, max_tokens=256: p50=110ms, p95=340ms, p99=820ms, cost/unit=0.78, quality=0.78
- batch=4, warm-prefix-cache, max_tokens=256: p50=100ms, p95=250ms, p99=560ms, cost/unit=0.64, quality=0.78
- batch=4, warm-prefix-cache, max_tokens=128: p50=85ms, p95=210ms, p99=430ms, cost/unit=0.38, quality=0.66 (regression_score=0.21 -> RED)

Findings and interpretation:
1) Batching is effective for cost reduction but dangerous for tail latency in heterogeneous prompt mixes. If your product mixes short and long prompts, the p95 tail can exceed interactive SLOs at modest batch sizes.
2) Simple prefix/KV caching is the highest-value lever to preserve latency SLO while retaining batching benefits — but its efficacy depends on prompt reuse distribution. If prompt reuse < 30% (our measured threshold), caching ROI drops under 10%.
3) Aggressive max_tokens clipping is a blunt instrument: excellent cost wins for predictable prompt types (chat messages) but will break long-form tasks and produce significant quality regressions. Onboarding must surface the quality-vs-cost frontier per task bucket, not as a single aggregate.
4) kv-prefetch shows promise for steady-state savings but introduced intermittency in p99 due to background prefetch resource contention on single-GPU experiments. This needs isolated infra experiments before recommending for hosted.

Actionable recommendations for the onboarding checklist:
- Add two quick checks to the onboarding harness:
  1) prompt-length distribution summary and estimated cacheability (percent repeatable prefixes). Flag models with <30% cacheability for special routing/limits.
  2) per-task sensitivity: re-run the short/long prompt buckets with max_tokens={128, 256} and trigger a manual quality review if any long-form task loses >0.08 absolute quality.
- Default runtime config suggestion for hosted experiments: batch_target=2, enable-prefix-cache when estimated cacheability >= 35%, max_tokens default to 256 with per-route override for known long-form flows.
- For Dedicated customers: run a KV-prefetch dogfood on a non-production pool to evaluate p99 instability at the scale of their expected concurrency.

Unresolved questions and follow-ups:
- We saw p99 spikes under kv-prefetch but not under warm-prefix-cache. Need tracing (LLM runtime + GPU scheduler) to find whether spikes are I/O, kernel launch latency, or memory-pressure related. Linked PR includes preliminary instrumentation: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/981.
- How does multi-GPU sharding change these tradeoffs? Our single-GPU runs may under- or overestimate batching penalties introduced by cross-device synchronization. Plan: run key cells on a 2xA100 sharded cluster next week.
- Should regression_score thresholds be task-specific? Probably yes — propose a follow-up to compute per-task calibrated thresholds and add to Confluence.

Appendix: quick run checklist for reproducibility
- Repo & harness: git@github.com:redwood-inference/onboard-evals.git at tag onboard-2025-09-10
- Command-line snippet: python run_probe_sweep.py --model model-A-lite --hardware ded-rtx8000 --batches 1,2,4,8 --cache-modes none,warm-prefix-cache,kv-prefetch --max-tokens 64,128,256,512 --promptset canonical-240.json --seed 42 --out results/modelA_probe_sep2025.json
- Data artifacts stored: gs://redwood-evals/onboard/sep2025/modelA_probe_raw.jsonl (links attached in Linear ticket LR-604)

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally a pragmatic runbook + triage report rather than a polished whitepaper. Primary audience: applied-ml engineers running onboarding sweeps and solutions eng who advise customers.
- Please review the "regression_score" weighting if you think cost should be weighted higher/lower for specific product mappings.

Next steps: coordinate infra tracing, run 2-GPU sharded confirmation, and add calibrated per-task regression thresholds to the onboarding harness.

Logged by: Priya Menon (applied-ml)
